mainEntity.name: How much does a Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid engine replacement typically costs £2,800-£5,500 for a rebuilt unit supply-only, with fitted prices ranging from £3,500-£7,500 depending on the engine code (DGEA 1.4 TSI vs 1.5 TSI eHybrid) and labour rates. Hybrid system calibration is included in specialist fitting. Used engines: £1,500-£4,200. Reconditioned: £2,500-£5,500. Rebuilt with warranty: £2,800-£6,500. Fitting labour: 10-14 hours at £65-£100/hr.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of 12V battery failure on a Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common signs include a '12V Battery Low' warning on the dashboard, the car not starting, or the car failing to charge. The 12V battery can discharge during charging, leaving the car unable to start. '12V Battery Low' warning. Car won't start after charging. 'E-Mode is currently unavailable' message. Orange warning light on the dash.

mainEntity.name: Does the Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid have a timing belt or chain?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 1.4 TSI engine in the eHybrid uses a timing chain. There has been a warranty extension for TSI timing chains and tensioners - 10 years or 100,000 miles (whichever comes first). Rattling noise on cold start is a common symptom of tensioner wear. Timing chain - not a belt (1.4 TSI). 10-year / 100,000-mile warranty extension may apply. Rattling on cold start: have it inspected immediately. Tensioner failure can cause catastrophic damage.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common problem on the Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common problems are 12V battery discharging during charging and DQ400e DSG mechatronic failure. The 12V battery drain is caused by the front assist camera and gateway constantly draining power. The DQ400e mechatronic unit can fail at 50,000-100,000+ miles. 12V battery drain: most common, often fixed by software update (90PV). DQ400e mechatronic failure: most expensive, £2,500-£4,000 replacement. Charging system incompatibility: affects 2024+ models. Overall reliability is very poor - 64.2% in What Car? survey.

mainEntity.name: Is the Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Tiguan eHybrid has been reported to have very poor reliability, scoring just 64.2% in the What Car? Reliability Survey - last out of 76 rivals in the family SUV category. Problems with the infotainment system were the most common, affecting 31% of cars, while faults with the braking system and non-engine electrical components each accounted for 19%. Very poor reliability - 64.2% score. 12V battery issues are common. DQ400e mechatronic failure is the most expensive risk. Regular servicing is critical for reliability.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the Tiguan eHybrid engine codes?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Tiguan eHybrid was offered with three main engine variants: DGEA (1.4 TSI, 2020-2023, 245 PS, 13 kWh battery), 1.5 TSI eHybrid 204 PS (2024-present, 19.7 kWh battery), and 1.5 TSI eHybrid 272 PS (2024-present, 19.7 kWh battery, top spec). DGEA: 1.4 TSI, 245 PS, 2020-2023, 31-mile range. 1.5 TSI eHybrid 204 PS: 1.5 TSI, 2024-present, 71-77-mile range. 1.5 TSI eHybrid 272 PS: 1.5 TSI, 2024-present, top spec.

historyTimeline.h2: Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid Plug-in Hybrid - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid was introduced in 2020 as the brand's plug-in hybrid SUV, combining a TSI petrol engine with an electric motor and a 13 kWh battery pack. The eHybrid replaced the GTE badge for the Tiguan range, though the GTE button remains for drivers to access all available power. The Tiguan is Volkswagen's best-selling model, making the eHybrid a key step in the brand's electrification strategy. The powertrain has evolved with a shift from the 1.4 TSI to the more modern 1.5 TSI EVO engine in the latest generation.

milestones.description: DGEA, 1.4-litre TSI plug-in hybrid, 245 PS (180 kW) combined - launch engine, 13 kWh battery, DQ400e 6-speed DSG, 31-mile electric range
1.4 TSI eHybrid with 245 PS - continued with minor software updates
1.5 TSI eHybrid (204 PS / 150 kW) introduced - 1.5-litre EVO engine, 19.7 kWh battery
1.5 TSI eHybrid (272 PS / 200 kW) introduced - top-spec plug-in hybrid
1.5 TSI eHybrid electric range increases to 71-77 miles

commonProblems.h2: Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid Plug-in Hybrid Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid is a sophisticated plug-in hybrid that combines a 1.4-litre or 1.5-litre TSI petrol engine with an electric motor and DQ400e 6-speed DSG gearbox. While the powertrain is generally well-regarded, it has specific, well-documented failure points - particularly around the 12V battery system, DQ400e gearbox, and charging system. The Tiguan eHybrid has been reported to have very poor reliability, scoring just 64.2% in the What Car? Reliability Survey - last out of 76 rivals in the family SUV category. Rebuilt engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure point, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: 12V Battery Discharging - The Most Common Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid Problem
problems.typicalFailureMileage: Unpredictable - can occur at any mileage
problems.rootCause: The 12V battery can discharge during charging, leaving the car unable to start. The problem is caused by the front assist camera and gateway constantly draining power - they don't turn off. One owner reported receiving a '12V Battery Low' warning every morning. A software update (campaign 90PV dated 12th Dec 24) is expected to fix the battery drain problem.

repairOptions.longevity: First step if battery is defective

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Apply Volkswagen software update to fix drain

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2020-2024 Tiguan eHybrid is worth £20,000-£48,000. A £180-£350 12V battery replacement is a minor expense. The software update is often free of charge if covered by a campaign.
problems.recommendation: 12V battery issues are the most common problem on the Tiguan eHybrid. If you see a "12V Battery Low" warning or the car won't start, have the 12V battery tested first. If the problem persists, check if the 90PV software update has been applied to your vehicle. Specialist hybrid diagnostic equipment is essential - not all garages can work on these systems.
problems.cta: -> Compare Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid hybrid diagnostic costs

problems.h4: DQ400e DSG Mechatronic Failure - Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid
problems.affectedModels: Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid (all variants, particularly DQ400e 6-speed)
problems.rootCause: The DQ400e gearbox is a six-speed dual-clutch transmission derived from the DQ250, with an added clutch and electric motor between the combustion engine and gearbox. The mechatronics unit is the DSG gearbox's Achilles heel, with many members reporting failures from 50,000-100,000+ miles. The oil strainer of the mechatronics can become dislodged under pressure, entering the N218 solenoid which controls the K0 clutch for starting the combustion engine.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Full DSG diagnostic, oil and filter change
repairOptions.longevity: First step; DSG service recommended every 40,000 miles
If gearbox has suffered catastrophic failure

problems.vehicleValueCheck: For a 2020-2024 Tiguan eHybrid worth £20,000-£48,000, a £2,500-£4,000 mechatronic replacement is a significant but justifiable repair if the car is otherwise sound.
problems.recommendation: DQ400e mechatronic failure is a known and expensive issue on the Tiguan eHybrid. Regular DSG servicing (every 40,000 miles) is critical to prevent premature failure. If you experience transmission warnings or rough shifting, have the car diagnosed immediately - catching the issue early may allow for a repair rather than a full replacement. Specialist DSG repair at £1,000-£1,800 is significantly cheaper than dealer prices.
problems.cta: -> Compare Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid DQ400e mechatronic replacement costs

problems.h4: Charging System & Wallbox Incompatibility - Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid
problems.affectedModels: Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid (all variants, particularly 2024+ 1.5 TSI models)
problems.typicalFailureMileage: Unpredictable - can occur at any mileage
problems.rootCause: The 2024 eHybrid has a larger battery and a CCS charging socket, but some public chargers see the car as the old Tiguan eHybrid with the smaller battery. It should accept 50kW max charge but doesn't. Scheduled charging is currently not possible to set, and the issue has been raised with Volkswagen many times. Incompatibilities with wallboxes have been reported.
problems.vehicleValueCheck: For a £20,000-£48,000 Tiguan eHybrid, these costs are relatively minor. A software update is often free.
problems.recommendation: Charging system issues are a growing concern for 2024+ eHybrid owners. If you're experiencing charging problems, check if a software update is available for your vehicle. Scheduled charging is expected to be resolved with a future software update. For wallbox compatibility issues, consult with your wallbox manufacturer.
